extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners and parties in PTAB inter partes review proceedings (petitioners, patent owners, and their counsel)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and legal criteria used by the Patent Trial and Appeal Board (PTAB) to analyze patentability challenges in an inter partes review (IPR), including claim construction, anticipation, obviousness, level of skill, and evidentiary burdens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdiction and authority for IPR decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board has jurisdiction to hear an inter partes review under 35 U.S.C. § 6; Final Written Decisions are issued pursuant to 35 U.S.C. § 318(a) and 37 C.F.R. § 42.73.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite the enabling statutory and regulatory authority when framing the proceeding and the Board’s power to render a Final Written Decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petitioner burden of proof (preponderance)
rubrics_metrics.description: In an inter partes review, the petitioner has the burden from the onset to show with particularity why the patent it challenges is unpatentable, and must demonstrate unpatentability by a preponderance of the evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The burden never shifts to the patentee (see 35 U.S.C. § 316(e)); petitions must identify with particularity the evidence supporting each ground (35 U.S.C. § 312(a)(3)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Petition particularity requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Inter partes review petitions must identify 'with particularity … the evidence that supports the grounds for the challenge to each claim' (35 U.S.C. § 312(a)(3)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Petitions must point to concrete evidence for each alleged claim deficiency; general assertions without specific supporting evidence are insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction standard (Phillips)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim terms are generally given their ordinary and customary meaning as understood by a person of ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention; look principally to intrinsic evidence (claim language, written description, prosecution history).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extrinsic evidence is less significant than intrinsic record in determining the legally operative meaning of claim language (Phillips v. AWH; DePuy Spine). Use specification and prosecution history first, then extrinsic evidence to aid understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weight of intrinsic vs extrinsic evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Intrinsic evidence (claims, specification, prosecution history) is primary; extrinsic evidence (expert testimony, dictionaries) is less significant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on intrinsic record for claim meaning; use extrinsic evidence only to assist and not to contradict intrinsic evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification-defined terms control
rubrics_metrics.description: When the specification expressly defines a claim term (e.g., 'fixed dose' defined in the specification), that definition governs and the term requires no further construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If parties do not dispute a specification definition, the Board will adopt the specification definition as the meaning of the claim term.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional claim language may be limiting
rubrics_metrics.description: Functional language in an apparatus claim can be limiting on claim scope (citing K-2 Corp.), rather than mere intended use, depending on the natural reading of the claim language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze whether the functional language informs structural requirements of the claimed device; if so, treat it as a limiting functional limitation rather than an unlimiting intended use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intended use vs structural limitation (In re Casey guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: A recited intended use of a device is not automatically given patentable weight (In re Casey), but functional language that imposes structural capability requirements may be limiting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not import method-of-treatment limitations from claim language that recites intended use unless the language naturally requires structural or functional capability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of 'delivers to a patient' (functional limitation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The phrase 'delivers to a patient' is construed as a functional limitation requiring that the claimed subcutaneous administration device be capable of containing and subcutaneously delivering the dose to a person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not import additional limitations (e.g., limited to patients with a specific disease or requiring 'safe and effective' delivery) unless the claim language supports them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of 'contains and delivers … 162 mg fixed dose' (no single-injection requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims reciting 'a subcutaneous administration device, which contains and delivers to a patient a 162 mg fixed dose' require the device to be capable of containing and delivering the 162 mg fixed dose subcutaneously but do not require that the dose be delivered in a single injection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The plain claim language controls; the common meaning of 'dose' (e.g., 'taken at one time') does not necessarily mandate a single physical injection—multiple sequential injections delivering the total amount can be within scope unless the claim expressly restricts method of delivery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Level of ordinary skill in the art (POSA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define POSA consistent with the problems addressed and the prior art; here the Board adopted an individual with several years experience researching treatments for autoimmune disorders (including RA) who would have access to individuals skilled in clinical medicine, pharmacokinetics, and formulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider applicant/inventor qualifications and prior art to set the POSA; POSA definition can affect obviousness/enablement analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation standard (single reference, express or inherent)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is anticipated only if each and every element is found, either expressly or inherently described, in a single prior art reference. A reference can anticipate even if it does not expressly spell out all limitations if a POSA would 'at once envisage' the arrangement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate that a single reference discloses every claim limitation, either expressly or inherently; unsubstantiated inferences that a reference implies an element are insufficient unless a POSA would immediately recognize the claimed combination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness standard and Graham factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Under 35 U.S.C. § 103, obviousness is determined by Graham factors: (1) scope and content of the prior art; (2) differences between claimed subject matter and the prior art; (3) level of ordinary skill in the art; and (4) objective evidence of nonobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also consider whether there was a motivation to combine references and whether a POSA would have had a reasonable expectation of success; apply KSR guidance (including 'obvious to try' when there are a finite number of predictable solutions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivation to combine / reasonable expectation of success
rubrics_metrics.description: When an obviousness determination relies on combining references, there must be some suggestion or motivation in the prior art to combine them, and a reasonable expectation of success must be founded in the prior art, not applicant disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show explicit or implicit motivation from prior art teachings or market/design pressures; avoid relying on hindsight or applicant’s own disclosure as the source of motivation or expectation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Printed publication / public accessibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a reference is a 'printed publication' depends on public accessibility; the Board may credit testimony (e.g., regarding ClinicalTrials.gov) establishing that the reference was publicly accessible as of the relevant date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate public accessibility (site design, intended public audience, witness credibility); documentation and witness testimony about how and when material was accessible are probative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apparatus claims are not limited by efficacy or safety
rubrics_metrics.description: Device/apparatus claims directed to an article of manufacture are not necessarily limited by claims of efficacy or therapeutic effect (i.e., they need not recite safety/effectiveness that would be required for method-of-treatment claims).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid importing efficacy/safety requirements into apparatus claims unless the claim language or specification clearly impose such limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art can reflect the appropriate level of skill
rubrics_metrics.description: The prior art itself can reflect the appropriate level of ordinary skill in the art and inform how a POSA would read references and combine teachings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use prior art content and context to help define POSA and reasonable expectations, rather than relying solely on expert labels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert testimony qualification and weight
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board reviews credentials of declarants and considers them qualified to provide opinions if credentials support expertise; the credibility of expert testimony affects weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide full credentials and a clear basis for opinions; the Board will credit testimony to the extent experts are demonstrably qualified and their opinions are supported by the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of prosecution history in claim interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Prosecution history (e.g., addition of claim language like 'contains') can inform claim meaning but cannot be used to import limitations beyond the claim language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine amendments and statements during prosecution for how the patentee distinguished claims, but do not extend claim scope by reading in unrecited limitations from prosecution remarks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obvious-to-try analysis (KSR guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a design need or market pressure exists and there are a finite number of identified, predictable solutions, trying the known options with a reasonable expectation of success can support a finding of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show that the options were limited and predictable and that a POSA would have had good reason to pursue them; but ensure this is grounded in prior art/motivation rather than hindsight.
